title: Replacement analysis and risk
subtitle: When is an old machine worth keeping, and how sure are we of any of these numbers?

sections.title: Why and when to replace
sections.body: Assets are replaced because of physical deterioration (rising maintenance), obsolescence (better technology) or changed requirements. The decision compares the current asset, the defender, with the best available replacement, the challenger. Use today’s market value of the defender as its investment — what you forgo by keeping it. What you paid for it long ago is a sunk cost.

questions.prompt: The defender’s original purchase price should be…

choices.text: Ignored; use its current market value.

sections.title: Comparing by equivalent annual cost
sections.body: Defender: market value 20,000 now, 3 more years, operating cost 6,000/yr, salvage 8,000. Challenger: 60,000, 6 years, operating cost 2,000/yr, salvage 10,000. MARR 10 %. Equivalent annual cost EAC = P·(A/P) + AOC − S·(A/F). Defender: Rs 11,625; challenger: Rs 14,480. The lower EAC wins: keep the defender.

worked.why: Capital recovery of 60,000 over 6 years at 10 %.
Add operating cost, subtract the salvage credit.

sections.title: Economic life
sections.eyebrow: When to stop using an asset
sections.body: As an asset ages its maintenance rises and its salvage falls. The economic life is the retention period that minimises the equivalent annual cost. For a 50,000 machine with falling salvage and rising maintenance at 10 %, the annual cost over n years is: 1 yr 24,000; 2 yr 20,429; 3 yr 19,483; 4 yr 19,315; 5 yr 19,542. The minimum is at 4 years (Rs 19,315).

worked.why: Evaluate for n = 1…5 and pick the smallest: n = 4.

questions.prompt: The economic life is the period that…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Before it, capital cost dominates; after it, upkeep does.

sections.title: Replacement over a finite horizon
sections.body: Assuming identical replacements forever is a modelling choice. If the planning horizon is finite (a 4-year contract) compare the cash flows over exactly that horizon, including the salvage at its end. Technology that improves rapidly favours shorter horizons and leasing.

questions.prompt: Which assumption underlies the EAC comparison of unequal-life machines?

sections.title: Risk and uncertainty
sections.body: Every input is an estimate. Sensitivity analysis changes one input at a time (±20 %) to see which matters most; scenario analysis changes sets of inputs together (best / expected / worst); probabilistic analysis gives inputs distributions and finds the distribution of the outcome. The expected value of an outcome is Σ p·x.

worked.why: Project NPW: +40,000 with prob 0.3, +10,000 with prob 0.5, −20,000 with prob 0.2.

questions.prompt: Expected value of a risky project is…

sections.title: NPW as a random variable
sections.body: If the NPW is roughly normal with mean Rs 12,000 and standard deviation Rs 9,000, the chance of a loss is P(NPW < 0) = Φ(−μ/σ) = Φ(−1.33) ≈ 9.12 %. A project can have a positive expected value and still carry a one-in-ten chance of losing money; decision-makers weigh that risk against the return. Adding many independent projects reduces the relative spread — diversification, the central limit theorem at work (means of 30 draws have sd 0.184).

sections.title: Monte Carlo on cash flows
sections.body: Give each uncertain input a distribution (demand ~ N(1000, 100), price ~ uniform 40–60), draw values many times, compute the NPW each time, and read the distribution: mean, spread, probability of loss. The error in any estimated probability shrinks like 1/√n, so 10,000 trials give about 1 % precision.
